title: Who disciplines whom
ask: Who disciplines a sitting Justice, a lower-court judge, a court employee and a lawyer?
items: Sitting SC Justice: impeachment only (In re Gonzalez)
Retired Justice: the Court, administratively (Biraogo)
Lower-court judges and CA Justices: the Supreme Court en banc (Sec. 11)
Court employees: the Supreme Court through the OCA; the CSC only files (Andal)
Lawyers: the Supreme Court (Gadon)
src: Art. VIII, Secs. 6 and 11; Art. XI, Sec. 2

title: What Maceda v. Vasquez held
ask: State the holdings of Maceda v. Vasquez (1993).
items: The SC has exclusive administrative supervision over all courts and personnel (Sec. 6)
One act may bring administrative and criminal liability
The Ombudsman has jurisdiction over the crime
But a criminal complaint arising from court duties must be referred to the Court first
The Court decides whether the respondent acted within his administrative duties
The Ombudsman cannot compel the Court to produce records or its personnel to testify

title: What CSC v. Andal held
ask: State the holdings of CSC v. Andal (2009).
items: Only the SC oversees court personnel’s compliance with all laws, rules and regulations
The CSC cannot try and decide administrative cases against court personnel
Not even for civil service exam anomalies
The CSC files its complaint with the OCA (Ampong)
No estoppel: he denied the charge, never appeared, and raised jurisdiction on appeal

title: Judges disciplined: the cases
ask: Give the cases where the Court disciplined Justices of the CA or the Court itself, with the penalty.
items: In re Demetria (2001): CA Justice who lobbied prosecutors, dismissed
Re: Vasquez (2008): Roxas dismissed; Sabio suspended two months; Reyes reprimanded; Dimaranan-Vidal admonished; Vasquez severely reprimanded
In re Biraogo (2009): retired Justice Reyes fined ₱500,000 and disqualified for a leaked ponencia
src: Art. VIII, Sec. 6; Code of Judicial Conduct

title: What In re Gadon held
ask: State the holdings of In re Gadon (2023).
items: No inhibition: bias needs clear and convincing proof; the Court acts as a collegial body
Baseless bias claims are direct contempt
Disbarment is sui generis: a fitness inquiry
Preventive suspension may come before the answer when the act speaks for itself
A lawyer cannot divide his personality: private conduct counts
Scandalous, misogynistic speech violates CPRA Canon II; disbarred

title: Change of venue: the rule and the cases
ask: When will the Court change the venue of a trial? Give the cases.
items: Art. VIII, Sec. 5(4): to avoid a miscarriage of justice
Not for whimsical or flimsy reasons; crimes are best tried where committed
Serious and weighty reasons to doubt a fair and impartial trial (People v. Gutierrez)
Pilotin: hostile sentiment endangering the accused’s life
Mondiguing: a judge tied to the victim; danger to the accused
Sola: the effect of fear on the witnesses; doubts favor the change
It may be sought administratively, and moves the whole record
src: Art. VIII, Sec. 5(4); Pilotin; Mondiguing; Sola

title: The SC’s administrative powers in Sec. 5 and 6
ask: List the Supreme Court’s administrative powers under Article VIII.
items: Administrative supervision over all courts and personnel (Sec. 6)
Temporary assignment of lower-court judges, at most six months without consent (Sec. 5(3))
Change of venue or place of trial (Sec. 5(4))
Appointment of all Judiciary officials and employees under the Civil Service Law (Sec. 5(6))
Discipline and dismissal of lower-court judges (Sec. 11)
